# Benchmarks as Measurement Contracts {#sec-benchmarks}

A benchmark score is not a property of model weights alone. It is the result of
running one model revision through one harness (the code that turns each test
case into a model call and parses the reply), on one version of a test set, with
one scorer and aggregation rule. Change any of those inputs and the number may
change. A useful report therefore begins with the claim the evaluation is meant
to support, then preserves enough evidence for someone else to reconstruct that
claim.

This chapter calls the written record of those inputs, tied to the claim they
support, a measurement contract. It explains how to choose test cases, keep them
separate from development, pin the execution harness, audit the answer key, and
retain per-case records. The next chapter, @sec-statistical-reliability,
asks how much uncertainty remains after those choices have been made.

## Begin with the decision

Suppose a team asks, “Is the new model better?” No benchmark can answer that
question until *better* is made specific: better at answering whose questions,
under what conditions, at what cost, and for which decision. A multiple-choice
exam measures performance on its own questions; a claim of general
intelligence, production usefulness, or safety needs further evidence.
Raji et al. call out this gap between a benchmark's narrow task and the broad
construct it is often made to represent, meaning the general ability the score
is taken to stand for [@raji2021everything].

Write the intended claim before choosing the test:

> For English-language support requests from the last quarter, using the
> production prompt and retrieval stack, model B resolves more cases than model
> A without regressing policy compliance or exceeding the latency budget.

That sentence identifies a population, a system boundary, a comparison, and
guardrails. It also shows that no single public benchmark can settle the
decision. Public suites remain useful for external comparison and regression
testing, but product claims need samples that resemble the product. The
evidence-centered benchmark design framework makes this order explicit: define
the capability and intended use, justify the content, document how the model is
adapted or prompted, assemble enough representative items, and explain how
item-level evidence becomes a test-level conclusion [@liu2024ecbd].

The common benchmark families are implementations of different measurement
choices, not interchangeable measures of one capability:

| Test form | What it can observe | Important limitation |
|---|---|---|
| Closed-answer questions, such as MMLU, GPQA, or Humanity's Last Exam [@hendrycks2020mmlu; @rein2023gpqa; @phan2025hle] | Correctness on a fixed academic sample | The sample may be unrepresentative, exposed, or mislabeled |
| Executable tasks, such as HumanEval, SWE-bench, or its human-validated subset SWE-bench Verified [@chen2021humaneval; @jimenez2023swebench; @openai2024swebenchverified] | Whether generated code passes a specified test environment | Tests and environment only approximate software quality |
| Synthetic probes, such as the configurable long-context tasks of RULER [@hsieh2024ruler] | A controlled mechanism under chosen conditions | Synthetic regularity may not transfer to natural inputs |
| Human preference comparisons, such as Chatbot Arena [@chiang2024chatbot] | Which output selected raters prefer | Preference depends on raters, rubric, presentation, and context |
| Interactive environments, such as GAIA, WebArena, or $\tau$-bench [@mialon2023gaia; @zhou2023webarena; @yao2024taubench] | Whether an agent reaches a defined state | Success also depends on tools, environment state, and repeated-run reliability |

Breadth helps only when the suite's composition matches the claim. The
“benchmark lottery” describes how conclusions and rankings can change with the
chosen tasks, datasets, and metrics [@dehghani2021benchmarklottery]. Adding
unrelated tests can make a dashboard larger while making its meaning less clear.

Several families also report on a decision made in an earlier layer of the
stack. Math benchmarks from grade-school GSM8K to competition-level MATH have
answers a program can check [@cobbe2021verifiers; @hendrycks2021math], the
property that lets the same problems serve as rewards in the verifiable-reward
training of @sec-training-to-reason. Running one task in several languages
exposes tokenizer and data-mixture choices from @sec-data-curation that stay
invisible while a model is measured only in English. Long-context probes gate
the context extension described in @sec-structured-long-context. MMMU tests
college-level subject knowledge over diagrams, charts, tables, and images
[@yue2023mmmu], a construct that captioning accuracy does not cover. The
interactive row is the subject of @sec-evaluating-agents, because an agent's
result is a changed environment state rather than a single answer.

## The decision also chooses the metric

Naming the decision also settles what to score, and the two decisions a
benchmark usually serves call for opposite properties. A release gate needs the
quantity the product is judged on, which is usually accuracy on parsed final
answers. A development decision, such as which data mixture or which of two
training runs to keep, is made on small models and on partly trained
checkpoints, the weight snapshots saved during a training run, where accuracy is
a coarse instrument: a multiple-choice score can sit near chance while the model
is in fact improving, and it moves between adjacent checkpoints of the same run
for no reason connected to model quality.

Heineman et al. turn that observation into two measurable properties of a
benchmark paired with a metric. **Signal** measures how well the pair separates
stronger models from weaker ones. **Noise** measures how much it moves between
training steps within a single run. Write $s_m$ for the score of model $m$ across
a set of models, $\sigma_{\mathrm{models}}$ for the standard deviation of
$\{s_m\}$, and $\sigma_{\mathrm{step}}$ for the standard deviation of the score
over the final checkpoints of one run. Signal is $\sigma_{\mathrm{models}}$,
noise is $\sigma_{\mathrm{step}}$, and their ratio

$$
\mathrm{SNR}=\frac{\sigma_{\mathrm{models}}}{\sigma_{\mathrm{step}}}
$$

indicates whether an observed gap carries information: a high ratio means the
spread between models is large relative to the fluctuation within one run. The
ratio as written gives the form of the comparison; the paper's own estimator
differs in detail. Across 30 benchmarks and 375 open-weight models from 60M to
32B parameters, they report that pairs with a higher ratio support more reliable
comparisons at small scale and produce better scaling-law fits. Three
interventions follow from the measurement: prefer a metric with a better ratio,
which for many benchmarks means per-token loss over the answer string (the
negative log-probability the model assigns to the reference answer, averaged
over its tokens) rather than accuracy on it; drop subtasks that contribute noise
to an aggregate; and average adjacent checkpoints to reduce
$\sigma_{\mathrm{step}}$ directly [@heineman2025signal].

```{figure}
//| figure: benchmark-snr
//| label: fig-benchmarks-snr
//| fig-cap: "Simulated scores, illustrative and not the cited study's data: six training runs of increasing model size answer one four-option benchmark, each scored at its last ten checkpoints by accuracy and by per-token loss on the reference answers. Each column is one run; its line joins the checkpoints in training order, and the larger dot is the final score $s_m$. In the simulation a model's general fluency raises the probability of every option and only its discrimination lifts the reference answer above the three distractors, so for small models accuracy stays near chance while loss still improves with size. The bars compare $\sigma_{\mathrm{models}}$, the spread of the six final scores, with $\sigma_{\mathrm{step}}$, the spread across one run's checkpoints; their ratio is the SNR. Averaging adjacent checkpoints shrinks $\sigma_{\mathrm{step}}$ for both metrics."
```

Loss is a development instrument, so the two decisions keep separate metrics. A
checkpoint that assigns higher probability to the reference answer can still
emit it in a form the parser rejects, and no product claim rests on per-token
loss. The two metrics answer different questions on the same items, and a
report that gives only one of them leaves the other decision without evidence.
@sec-statistical-reliability supplies the intervals for deciding when a gap on
either metric is large enough to act on.

## Specify the evaluation object

An evaluation should be a versioned artifact whose specification pins, at
minimum, the data, model, harness, and scorer:

```text
EvaluationSpec:
  benchmark_id, benchmark_revision, item_manifest_hash
  model_id, model_revision, tokenizer_revision
  prompt_template_revision, system_policy_revision
  few_shot_policy, tool_environment_revision
  decoding_parameters, seeds, repetitions
  scorer_revision, normalization, exclusion_policy
  contamination_audit_revision, run_environment

EvaluationCase:
  case_id, source, license, created_at, language, domain
  input_hash, reference_hash, rubric_revision
  slice_labels, dependencies, leakage_status

EvaluationRecord:
  spec_hash, case_id, attempt, raw_output_hash
  parsed_output, score, scorer_trace
  latency, token_cost, tool_cost
```

`EvaluationSpec` says how the run behaves. `EvaluationCase` documents what an
item represents. `EvaluationRecord` preserves
what happened. An aggregate score can be recomputed from those records; it
cannot recreate them after they have been discarded. Dataset documentation has
the same purpose at a broader scale: it makes motivation, composition,
collection, recommended uses, and limitations inspectable rather than implicit
[@gebru2021datasheets].

Let $y_i$ be the score on case $i$, let $w_i \ge 0$ be its predeclared weight,
and let $n$ be the number of cases. The reported weighted mean is

$$
\widehat{\mu} =
\frac{\sum_{i=1}^{n} w_i y_i}{\sum_{i=1}^{n} w_i}.
$$

Here, $i$ identifies one evaluation case, $y_i$ may be binary correctness or a
numeric rubric score, $w_i$ controls how much that case contributes, and
$\widehat{\mu}$ is the estimated mean for the population implied by those
weights. Equal weights do not mean “no assumption”; they assume every sampled
case should contribute equally.

For a comparison on the same cases, retain
$d_i = y_i^{(B)} - y_i^{(A)}$, the case-level difference between systems B and
A, and aggregate the $d_i$ values. This paired record shows whether B fixed A's
failures or traded them for different ones. If a stochastic code or agent task
is attempted repeatedly, average or model repetitions within the task before
treating tasks as independent units. Twenty attempts on one repository are not
twenty independent repositories. @sec-statistical-reliability develops the
appropriate intervals and tests.

The score comes last and is computed from several versioned decisions; the
evidence is the per-case records it summarizes.

## Held out from what?

A @gls-held-out is data deliberately kept out of every training stage; it is a
pipeline contract, not a property a file can prove by itself. In a closed
training pipeline, the contract can cover pre-training, supervised tuning,
preference data, synthetic-data generation, prompt selection, and checkpoint
selection. For an external model trained on undisclosed web data, an evaluator
usually cannot establish that a public test was never seen. The status to record
is “exposure unknown,” not “clean.”

Several different failures are often compressed into the word contamination:

1. **Training leakage:** an input, answer, or close duplicate enters pre-training
   or later training data.
2. **Indirect leakage:** synthetic examples inherit benchmark content from a
   teacher or retrieval source (@sec-synthetic-data), so a clean corpus does
   not protect a student trained on a dirty teacher's output.
3. **Development leakage:** prompts, parsers, checkpoints, or policies are
   repeatedly chosen against evaluation results.
4. **Reporting leakage:** items are filtered or reinterpreted after outputs are
   visible, without the exclusions appearing in the report.

The third failure is ordinary adaptive overfitting. A test set stops acting like
fresh evidence when developers query it, change the system, and query it again.
The reusable-holdout literature formalized this problem for adaptive data
analysis: repeated access needs controlled disclosure or fresh data if validity
is to survive [@dwork2015reusable]. A private final set, accessible only to a
release service, can preserve one last independent check. It is not permanently
trustworthy; access history and prior decisions determine how much independence
remains.

The selection effect is large even when nothing improves. The cell below gives
$k$ prompt or checkpoint variants the same true accuracy $p$, scores all of them
on one reused test set of $n$ cases, keeps the top scorer, and then scores the
kept variant on fresh cases. On the reused set the kept variant sits
$\sigma\,\mathbb{E}[\max_k Z]$ above $p$, where $\sigma=\sqrt{p(1-p)/n}$ is the
sampling error of one score and $\mathbb{E}[\max_k Z]$ is the expected maximum of
$k$ standard normal draws; the code checks the simulation against that closed
form. With 400 cases, trying 100 variants reports a gain of about six points
that fresh cases do not reproduce. Raising `n` to 4000 shrinks the invented
gain by a factor of about three, the square root of ten, but does not remove it.

:::: {.runnable}
```python
import math
import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
n, p, runs = 400, 0.70, 4000     # test cases, true accuracy of every variant, repeated experiments
K = np.array([1, 2, 3, 5, 10, 20, 50, 100])   # variants tried against the same test set

kept_test, kept_fresh = [], []
for k in K:
    test = rng.binomial(n, p, size=(runs, k)) / n    # every variant scored on one reused set
    kept_test.append(test.max(axis=1).mean())        # the team keeps the top scorer
    kept_fresh.append((rng.binomial(n, p, size=runs) / n).mean())  # its score on unseen cases
kept_test, kept_fresh = np.array(kept_test), np.array(kept_fresh)

# Closed form: the best of k equal variants sits sigma * E[max of k standard normals] above p.
sigma = math.sqrt(p * (1 - p) / n)
z = np.linspace(-6, 6, 4001)
Phi = 0.5 * (1 + np.array([math.erf(v / math.sqrt(2)) for v in z]))
phi = np.exp(-z**2 / 2) / math.sqrt(2 * math.pi)
e_max = np.array([(z * k * phi * Phi**(k - 1)).sum() * (z[1] - z[0]) for k in K])
predicted = p + sigma * e_max

assert np.allclose(kept_test, predicted, atol=0.15 * sigma)   # the inflation is pure selection
assert np.all(np.abs(kept_fresh - p) < 0.1 * sigma)           # fresh cases see no gain
print(f"k=100: reused set {kept_test[-1]:.3f}, fresh cases {kept_fresh[-1]:.3f}, true {p:.3f}")

plt.figure(figsize=(6, 3.6))
plt.semilogx(K, 100 * kept_test, "o-", label="kept variant, reused test set")
plt.semilogx(K, 100 * predicted, "k--", lw=1, label="closed form")
plt.semilogx(K, 100 * kept_fresh, "s-", label="kept variant, fresh cases")
plt.xlabel("variants tried against one test set, k")
plt.ylabel("accuracy (%)")
plt.title("Keeping the best of k equal variants invents a gain")
plt.legend(frameon=False)
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()
```
::::

Training leakage can pass for capability. SWE-bench builds its tasks from
public GitHub issues, and state-of-the-art models named the file to repair from
the issue text alone, without seeing the repository, up to 76 percent of the
time; on repositories outside the benchmark the same probe reached at most
53 percent [@liang2025swebenchillusion]. The gap points to memorized benchmark
content, and the headline repair score does not show it.

Audits provide evidence about exposure, not proof of absence. Exact hashes and
n-gram matching find exact or near duplicates when the training corpus is
available. Canaries reveal ingestion when a model reproduces a unique planted
string. @gls-membership-inference, tests that ask whether a specific example was
in the training data, can probe weights without access to the corpus. Min-K%
Prob, for example, uses unusually high probabilities on a text's least likely
tokens as a membership signal [@shi2023detecting]. Its ICLR study evaluates a
detection method under particular data and model conditions; a negative result
does not certify that an item was unseen.

Record the audit's scope in the status itself: `known_overlap`,
`suspected_overlap`, `no_overlap_found_under_audit_X`, or `not_auditable`.
Calling a case `clean` after one detector returns a negative result discards
that scope, which is the qualification the negative result depends on.

Each publication policy protects one property by giving up another:

| Design | Strength | Cost or risk |
|---|---|---|
| Public, static set | Reproducible and independently runnable | Easy to study, tune against, and ingest into later corpora |
| Private, static set | Limits direct access | Harder to audit; repeated submissions still adapt to it |
| Rotating or newly sourced set | Reduces exposure to older training data | Scores across revisions are less directly comparable |
| Generated or live environment | Can sample many fresh states | Generator, judge, and environment introduce new biases |

LiveBench is one example of rotating questions with automatic grading
[@white2024livebench]. Its design reduces some exposure risks; it does not make
the questions representative, the scorer correct, or comparisons across changing
revisions automatic. “Fresh” and “valid” answer different questions.

## Audit the instrument

Even a test that never entered training can be wrong. Items may have incorrect
keys, ambiguous wording, stale facts, broken dependencies, or a parser that rejects a
valid answer. MMLU-Redux manually re-annotated 5,700 MMLU questions and estimated
that 6.49% contained errors, with large variation among subjects
[@gema2024mmluredux]. Humanity's Last Exam, built from expert-written questions
at the edge of academic knowledge, shows the same problem on a harder test.
FutureHouse checked 321 of its text-only chemistry and biology questions against
the literature and found that 29 ± 3.7 percent (95 percent interval) had
reference answers directly contradicted by peer-reviewed evidence; the
maintainers' own three-expert review of a subset put the share near 18 percent
[@futurehouse2025hle]. HLE-Verified later re-examined all 2,500 items: 668 passed
as written, 1,143 were revised, and 689 remained uncertain. Eight models scored
7 to 10 points higher on the revised set, and 30 to 40 points higher on the
items whose statement or reference answer had been wrong [@zhai2026hleverified].

A wrong key does not flatter a model the way leakage does. If a fraction $e$ of
the keys is wrong, a model that answers every item correctly scores at most
$1-e$, and a model that reproduces the key's mistake is rewarded for it. The
answer key is therefore an input that can be wrong, and it needs the same audit
as the rest of the benchmark.

Before using a suite as a release gate, audit a sample of cases and every case
that changes the decision. Check:

- whether the prompt has one defensible interpretation;
- whether the reference answer and rationale agree;
- whether alternative valid forms survive normalization and parsing;
- whether duplicates or shared sources make cases dependent;
- whether dates, tools, packages, websites, and repositories are still valid;
- whether language, domain, difficulty, and user slices cover the intended
  population;
- whether licenses and access terms allow the proposed use; and
- whether exclusions were declared before results were examined.

Keep an adjudication log. Correcting an item creates a new benchmark revision;
silently changing the key under the old name destroys comparability. Also run
simple baselines: random choice where applicable, a trivial lexical heuristic,
the previous production system, and an oracle or qualified human estimate when
one is meaningful. A sophisticated model losing to a trivial heuristic often
reveals a shortcut in the test rather than a subtle model failure.

Maintainers of public benchmarks now apply the same revision rule to
their own suites and publish fixes as numbered versions of a benchmark that
stays in use. Terminal-Bench, a suite of command-line tasks graded inside
containers, versions each task semantically. A patch that cannot affect scores
lets earlier runs be reused, a change to the verifier alone lets saved runs be
regraded, and a change to the agent's environment requires new runs; a dataset's
version bump matches the largest bump among its tasks [@tbench2026continuous;
@tbench2026v4]. $\tau$-bench, which scores tool-using agents in simulated
customer-service conversations, states in its release notes which domains'
scores are not comparable across a release [@sierra2026taubench101]. Humanity's
Last Exam, a set of expert-written closed-answer questions, now has
HLE-Rolling, a continually updated fork (@sec-capability-horizon)
[@scale2026hleleaderboard]. A maintained benchmark stays useful for longer, and
it changes what a reported score has to carry. The same benchmark name can
cover several task sets on which one system scores differently, so a score
names the benchmark version, and a comparison across versions rests on a rerun,
a regrade, or the maintainer's statement that the change preserves scores.

::: {.callout-note .dated}
## As of September 2026

Terminal-Bench 2.1, released on 6 May 2026, fixed 28 of the 89 tasks in version
2.0 whose external dependencies had drifted, whose resource budgets were too
small, or whose instructions disagreed with their tests. Claude Opus 4.6
running in Claude Code scored 58.0 percent on 2.0 and 70.1 percent on 2.1
[@tbench2026v21]. Terminal-Bench 4.0, released on 28 August 2026, removed 8
tasks and fixed 19 [@tbench2026v4]. $\tau$-bench 1.0.0, of 18 March 2026, fixed more
than 75 tasks [@sierra2026taubench100]; $\tau$-bench 1.0.1, of 22 July 2026,
corrected a grading error in its banking domain, and regrading the stored
leaderboard runs raised single-attempt scores by up to about nine points
[@sierra2026taubench101]. CAIS released the 17 September 2026 version of
HLE-Rolling [@scale2026hleleaderboard].
:::

## The harness is part of the measured system

The same weights can produce different scores under different prompt templates,
few-shot examples (worked examples placed in the prompt ahead of the question),
chat templates, decoding settings, tool versions, and answer parsers.
Standardized frameworks such as @gls-helm make these choices explicit and
evaluate more than accuracy, improving comparison and auditability
[@liang2022helm]. Standardization fixes one harness so that participants are
measured under the same declared conditions; that harness remains part of every
score it produces.

That creates two legitimate but different experiments:

- A **controlled model comparison** fixes the harness as far as possible and
  asks how model revisions differ under the same interface.
- A **best-system comparison** permits model-specific prompting or tools and asks
  how complete deployed systems differ under a shared budget and task contract.

Do not label the second as a comparison of weights. Conversely, forcing every
model through a prompt format poorly matched to its training may answer a
well-controlled but operationally unhelpful question. State which experiment is
being run.

The scorer needs the same discipline. Preserve raw output before parsing, record
the parser and scorer revision, and distinguish `invalid`, `unknown`, `timeout`,
and `scorer_error` from an ordinary wrong answer. A model-based judge adds its
own model revision, prompt, order effects, and stochasticity; @sec-judging-holistic
develops that case. A test runner adds container images, dependencies, clocks,
network state, and flaky tests. Automatic grading still involves interpretation:
the parser, the judge, and the test environment each encode a choice about what
counts as correct.

::: {.callout-important}
## What's contested
Should every model receive exactly the same harness, or should each receive the
best harness its developer can build? A fixed harness improves attribution and
reproducibility. A model-specific harness may better estimate the best system a
user could deploy. The two numbers answer different questions, and each supports
only its own claim. The error is publishing either one without its harness and
then using it for the other claim.
:::

## Benchmarks decay

A fixed benchmark loses decision value through several independent processes:

- **Exposure:** cases or answers enter training and development loops.
- **Adaptive reuse:** repeated result-driven changes overfit the test even
  without direct training leakage.
- **Saturation:** scores cluster near the ceiling, leaving too little variation
  to separate systems.
- **Population drift:** the users, tasks, languages, or threats relevant to the
  decision change.
- **Scorer drift:** a formerly valid answer key, package, website, policy, or
  judge no longer represents the desired behavior.

@fig-benchmarks-1 illustrates saturation. The curves are schematic, and real
benchmarks saturate on different timelines. The figure shows how a bounded test
loses resolution when most systems succeed on almost every item.

![Schematic benchmark saturation. Successive systems approach the ceiling of a fixed test, reducing the score spread available to distinguish them; a harder successor restores headroom but begins its own lifecycle. The curves are illustrative, not measured results.](/figures/benchmarks-1.svg){#fig-benchmarks-1}

Saturation can be recognized from the scores themselves. The leading systems
sit within a few items of one another, a gap comparable to the sampling error
of a test with a few hundred items, and at or above a measured human reference
level. Inside that band a ranking says little about which system is more
capable; @sec-statistical-reliability gives the intervals that show how wide
the band is.

::: {.callout-note .dated}
## As of September 2026

GAIA's authors measured human respondents at 92 percent [@mialon2023gaia]. On
23 September 2026, fourteen entries on its test-set leaderboard, all
self-submitted systems scored against withheld answers, lay between 92.0 and
93.7 percent, a spread of five questions; the top entry, a system combining
several models, was added on 22 September [@gaia2026results]. GPQA Diamond has
198 graduate-level science questions, on which PhD-level experts recruited by
OpenAI scored 69.7 percent. In Epoch AI's independent runs, GPT-6 Astra scored
95.8 percent and seven other models scored between 94.0 and 95.4 percent, each
with a standard error of 1.3 to 1.7 points [@epoch2026gpqa].
:::

The succession of knowledge and reasoning tests follows this cycle. MMLU
separated models when it appeared [@hendrycks2020mmlu]. GPQA was then built to
be hard to look up: experts holding or pursuing a PhD in a question's field
reached 65 percent, while
skilled non-experts with unrestricted web access reached 34 percent, so
retrieval could not stand in for reasoning [@rein2023gpqa]. Humanity's Last Exam
moved to closed-ended questions written at the edge of expert knowledge
[@phan2025hle]. The ARC family took a different route. ARC-AGI-2 kept static
grid puzzles that humans solve and models find hard [@chollet2025arcagi2], and
ARC-AGI-3 replaced the answer key with interactive turn-based environments whose
rules an agent must discover by acting [@arcprize2026arcagi3]. Chatbot Arena
removed the fixed test set altogether: it ranks models from a stream of fresh
pairwise human votes, so there is no answer key to leak [@chiang2024chatbot],
and its rating then depends on which users vote and which prompts they bring,
as @sec-judging-holistic describes. Each step
gives up some comparability over time in exchange for resistance to exposure,
the trade the publication-policy table above describes.

Do not respond by adding harder questions blindly. Difficulty is useful only if
the new cases still represent the construct and decision. Maintain a benchmark
like a production dependency: record revisions, monitor item statistics and
coverage, retire broken cases, add newly relevant slices, and preserve a stable
anchor set when longitudinal comparison matters. Retirement can follow a stated
rule. Terminal-Bench 4.0, for example, removed tasks that every model of the
latest generation solved in five of five attempts, because such a task no
longer separates models [@tbench2026v4].

## Run, retain, and report

A defensible benchmark run can be implemented as a short procedure:

1. State the construct, population, intended use, primary metric, and
   guardrails.
2. Freeze the model, harness, scorer, item manifest, weights, exclusions, seeds,
   and repetition policy in an `EvaluationSpec`.
3. Audit provenance, rights, answer quality, dependencies, and exposure risk.
4. Run baselines and candidate systems under the declared comparison design.
5. Store raw outputs, parsed outputs, scorer traces, costs, and failures for
   every attempt.
6. Aggregate at the correct sampling unit; report paired changes, slices, and
   uncertainty.
7. Stress the instrument with format changes, option-order permutations,
   paraphrases, and environmental reruns where those should preserve meaning.
8. Apply only predeclared release rules, and log every exception or post-hoc
   analysis.

Four invariants make the procedure auditable: no evaluation case enters a
training or tuning path; no item disappears silently; raw output remains
immutable; and every reported number resolves to a spec hash and case-level
records. These rules make errors visible and repairable, which is a weaker
guarantee than validity.

A report should therefore lead with the qualified claim, not the largest score.
Name the benchmark revision, model and system boundary, harness, sample and
weights, scorer, known leakage and item defects, uncertainty, relevant slices,
and the decision the evidence supports. A leaderboard row omits most of this
context, so it should link to a result record rather than stand in for one.

A static benchmark is also one layer of evidence among several. Production
monitoring, A/B tests, user feedback, and human studies catch failures that a
fixed test set lets through, such as a shift in the user population, while a
static benchmark catches regressions before those slower layers see them.
Following the @gls-swiss-cheese, each layer has gaps, and confidence comes from
stacking layers whose gaps do not line up; @sec-operational-evaluation
assembles them into release gates.

::: {.callout-tip}
## Lower-layer constraint
Held-out integrity is decided below the evaluation layer. The data pipeline
(@sec-data-curation) must exclude protected cases and their near duplicates from
training mixtures, while the model registry, prompt registry, orchestration
layer, and serving traces must retain the revisions used in each run. Evaluation can define the contract and
audit the evidence, but it cannot reconstruct provenance that lower layers did
not preserve. If those layers lose lineage, a precise score can still be
uninterpretable.
:::

With the evaluation object defined, the next question is how stable its
aggregate is. @sec-statistical-reliability turns the saved case-level records
into intervals, paired comparisons, and release decisions without mistaking
precision for validity.
